answer.rationale: With the line at 94% of committed volume and no buffer, delivery risk is the binding constraint, and memory_c2 shows the low-cost switch alternative missed SLA in 3 of 4 quarters — unacceptable given zero slack. Memory_c1 and c6 suggest incumbent stability and multi-year commitments preserve service scope while cutting unit cost, and memory_c4 shows renegotiation at renewal previously recovered real margin without disrupting supply. Given the 18% spend-cut mandate and the 14-day contract expiry, negotiating terms with the incumbent (leveraging benchmarking and possibly a multi-year structure) addresses the cost mandate without introducing the delivery risk a vendor switch or new second-source onboarding would carry under current volume pressure. I verified memory_c4 (core evidence for negotiation efficacy) and memory_c2 (core evidence against switching under these conditions) since these two most directly bound the decision between the live options. Second-sourcing (c3) is valuable but is a separate, additive decision better suited to the next cycle given the one-decision constraint this round.
